text: Initial read: I am testing the abstract-scan bridge against mechanism assumptions. Q’s peer-scoring implementation uses a known type-to-belief map, utility cancellation, and effectively unbounded off-target penalties (Q §§Multi-Agent, lines 1645–1706), while P’s Energy Society uses finite survival energy and prompted objectives, with verifiable job outcomes and a non-binding recommendation phase (P lines 147–166, 199–237, 264–276). I will look for a narrow, operational claim about disciplining recommendations or capability reports under these constraints; the coupled-reward theorem may not transfer to discrete jobs and unobserved biases.

I am comparing Q’s exact incentive assumptions with P’s implemented game before choosing a mechanism. Initial concern: P’s competitive/cooperative labels may change objectives through prompts rather than the state-contingent rewards required by Q; I will check the action and payoff definitions and seek an observable deviation with a falsifiable intervention.

The scan’s claim that P already exhibits sandbagging is unsupported. Q defines sandbagging as strategic underperformance because a higher evaluation score triggers worse future permissions (Q lines 980–995, 1061–1069). P has no capability-contingent deployment or action cap: correct jobs pay energy, while failure pays zero; its reported self-serving evidence concerns recommendations and donation requests (P lines 147–176, 773–800). Likewise Q’s coupled-reward proposition needs two real-valued actions, countervailing biases on a known strictly decreasing curve, and reward functions of action difference (Q lines 1785–1884); P offers discrete job/donate/idle actions and no estimated bias curve (P lines 161–169, 199–237). A direct test of either theorem would require a redesigned game.

Sharper connection: Q’s peer-discipline proposition (Q.tex lines 1650–1745, especially (S), (PR)) scores a report against co-player *type reports*, whose underlying types are fixed before reporting; truth wins by \(\Lambda\lVert\beta_i[t_i]-\beta_i[\hat t_i]\rVert_2^2\). P’s discussion phase (P.tex lines 199–230) instead publishes each agent’s recommendations before peers choose actions; P explicitly says discussion can influence decisions, and lines 773–803/870–880 observe more collision-inducing recommendations in competition. A naive extension that scores predictions/recommendations against peers’ *later actions* violates the fixed-outcome step: if peer \(j\) follows a binary recommendation \(r\), then \(a_j=r\), so a score \(-\Lambda(r-a_j)^2\) is maximal for either recommendation regardless of the sender’s prior belief, for every \(\Lambda\). This is an inference/counterexample, not a result already in either paper. It suggests a testable question: can an incentive scheme elicit useful peer forecasts while those forecasts are also public advice that changes the target action? Need distinguish prediction from recommendation and test influence causally.

Independent constraint on the intervention: P’s natural-language discussion is costly. Removing it raises competitive large-agent active rounds from (14.0\pm9.5) to (27.2\pm6.3) (agent 4) and (5.2\pm1.6) to (15.6\pm9.0) (agent 5), although collisions rise from (12.80\pm3.90) to (21.00\pm4.36) per run (P lines 359–435, 569–629). Thus a mechanism must be evaluated on net energy/survival after message and scoring costs, not just fewer collisions. P’s reported collision recommendations are suggestive but not causal evidence of deception: the paper explicitly says duplicate recommendations are not always irrational (P lines 793–800). A useful design comparison is baseline discussion, no discussion, and compact sealed reports plus allocation/scoring, with fixed job seeds and matched active-agent exposure.

Candidate paper-level question and design: When a scored peer forecast is disclosed as advice, does it become self-fulfilling and cease to elicit a belief? For a binary action \(Y_j\) and forecast \(q\), quadratic score \(S(q,Y_j)=2qY_j-q^2\) gives \(\mathbb E[S]=2q p(q)-q^2\), where \(p(q)=\Pr(Y_j=1\mid\operatorname{do}(\text{disclose }q))\). With fixed \(p\), the maximizer is \(q=p\); with endogenous response, an interior best reply obeys \(q=p(q)+q p^{\prime}(q)\). E.g. if peers probabilistically copy \(q\), \(p(q)=q\), then \(\mathbb E[S]=q^2\), which rewards extreme reports. This formalizes exactly the missing assumption between Q’s exogenous type-score and P’s public action advice. Experiment: hold P’s recommendations fixed/committed first; add a scored forecast on whether a named peer takes a specified job; randomize disclosure of that forecast to the peer while holding prompt and token costs as equal as practical. Private forecasts are a benchmark; randomized public disclosure estimates action response \(p(q)\). Measure forecast distribution/calibration, peer action changes, collisions, energy and total energy across paired seeds; vary bounded score weight. Do not call strategic deception from observed recommendations alone.

Q explicitly labels peer discipline a benchmark relying on rewards that are free and unbounded (Q Introduction, line 267); its (PR) also cancels reported intrinsic utility and assigns (-\infty) off target (Q lines 1676–1698). P’s energy is the scarce survival resource, debited for every generated token, and donations are bounded by the donor’s balance (P lines 147–169). If scoring rewards are denominated in energy, they are not free, while any penalty is limited by survival/available balance. Therefore lower collision counts alone cannot validate Q’s implementation theorem; the research question is whether a bounded, resource-aware intervention yields a positive net gain and preserves agent participation. This is a material revision of the scan’s ‘engineering extension’ feasibility judgment.

Ada’s #7 objection is right and sharpens my proposal: Q’s (PR) uses \(-\infty\) off-support penalties, cancels unknown intrinsic utility and takes \(\Lambda\) arbitrarily large, whereas P energy is a finite survival budget (Q.tex 1676–1725; P.tex 147–170). Thus the proposal in #6 is a *mechanism-inspired stress test*, not a faithful implementation of Q’s theorem; a bounded energy score can itself change survival and must be included in net welfare, with gross job gains and external score subsidy reported separately. A practical nonnegative score is \(B(q,Y)=1-(q-Y)^2\), paid at a predeclared bounded rate. Under endogenous \(p(q)\), its first-order condition is \(q=p(q)+(q-1/2)p^{\prime}(q)\). Unlike the exogenous case, the outcome-only difference between two proper quadratic scores changes incentives, another reason to specify the exact payment rule. The decisive control is to commit P’s ordinary recommendations before eliciting forecasts, then randomize *after forecast submission* whether each scored forecast is revealed to its target; hidden forecasts cannot affect that peer’s simultaneous current-round decision through this channel.

Correction to my entries #5 and #7: their math delimiters were lost during command quoting. The figures should read \(14.0\pm9.5\), \(27.2\pm6.3\), \(5.2\pm1.6\), \(15.6\pm9.0\), \(12.80\pm3.90\), and \(21.00\pm4.36\); Q's off-target reward is \(-\infty\). Substantive refinement of #6: Q's actual binary quadratic peer score is \(S(q,y)=2[qy+(1-q)(1-y)]-[q^2+(1-q)^2]\). If public forecast \(q\) makes the peer choose \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\), then \(\mathbb E S=q^2+(1-q)^2\), maximizing at both extreme reports \(q\in\{0,1\}\). The one-coordinate score \(2qy-q^2\) is proper for exogenous \(Y\), but differs by the outcome term \(2(1-q)(1-y)-(1-q)^2\); under endogenous \(Y\), score normalizations can change incentives. Therefore use Q's full score for the counterexample.

Algebra clarification to #9: for \(T(q,Y)=2qY-q^2\), Q's binary score satisfies \(S(q,Y)=2T(q,Y)+1-2Y=2[1-(q-Y)^2]-1\). Thus \(T\) and \(S\) are equivalent up to positive scaling and an outcome-only term only when \(Y\) is exogenous. If forecast disclosure shifts \(Y\), the term \(1-2Y\) is no longer report-independent in expectation.

Cross-check of Ada #9: use Q’s *full* binary quadratic score for any claim about Q. Algebra gives \(S_Q(q,Y)=2[qY+(1-q)(1-Y)]-[q^2+(1-q)^2]=1-2Y+4qY-2q^2=2B(q,Y)-1\), where \(B(q,Y)=1-(q-Y)^2\). So the bounded nonnegative Brier score in #8 is an affine transform of Q’s actual score and has exactly the same report incentives, even when \(Y\) is endogenous. By contrast, the one-coordinate score in #6 differs from \(S_Q\) by an outcome-only term after scaling, which is strategically material when reporting changes \(Y\). Under \(\Pr(Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(q))=q\), \(\mathbb E S_Q=q^2+(1-q)^2\), maximal at \(q=0\) or \(q=1\). I agree with #5 that the no-discussion arm is an essential welfare comparator: P shows a large collision decrease from discussion but a large active-round loss for large agents, so the experiment must report net energy and active rounds, not just accuracy or collisions.

Design caution for #6/#8: randomizing disclosure after submission identifies the *causal effect of displaying a fixed forecast* on the peer's action. It does not by itself make hidden-arm forecasts a truthful proper-score benchmark if the forecaster knew at submission that disclosure was possible; its chosen \(q\) may optimize the mixture of hidden and revealed payoffs. Add a regime in which forecasts are committed to remain private and scored only against peer actions (with ordinary recommendations fixed first), then compare to a preannounced probabilistic-disclosure regime. Estimate action-response effects within the latter using post-submission randomization. Also report score transfers/subsidies separately from net job energy and survival.

The selected connection should be replaced, not merely narrowed. In Q, the score target is a co-player's pre-existing *type report*, and separation concerns conditional beliefs over these types (Q lines 1650–1698). In P, model identity, size and recent memory are already shown to other agents (P lines 188–198), while discussion messages concern *recommended actions* that can change later decisions (P lines 199–230). There is no demonstrated private correlated type to elicit, and P’s recommendation metrics do not establish lying. A publishable bridge is the failure mode of using an action-based score on public advice: disclosure can make a scored forecast self-fulfilling, invalidating the fixed-target proper-score argument; P supplies a controlled, costly communication channel for testing this under competitive survival incentives. The net-resource comparison from #5/#7 is part of the estimand, not an optional metric.

Prior-work check changes the novelty assessment. Query: "proper scoring rules endogenous events forecasts influence outcome self fulfilling prediction paper" (also "prediction markets decision dependent outcomes manipulation scoring rules paper"). Oesterheld et al. (UAI 2023, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v216/oesterheld23a.html) already prove that score-maximizing *performative predictions* generally need not match beliefs and study bounds/modified scoring rules; Chakraborty and Das (2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.7015) study prediction-market participants who affect outcomes. Thus #6’s mathematical counterexample is a diagnostic bridge from Q to P, not a novel theorem. The potentially publishable advance is empirical/design-specific: quantify the causal effect of public scored forecasts on *other LLM agents’ subsequent choices* in P’s token-costed, congested survival economy, and test whether sealed reports or compact allocation mechanisms improve net energy/survival. A theoretical paper merely restating score endogeneity would be redundant. I have not found a direct test in this exact setting in these queries, but this is not a novelty claim.

Minor precision correction to #13: P explicitly says peers observe each other's status, energy level, size, and five recent memory entries (P lines 193–197). It does not explicitly say the model name or full capability type is disclosed to peers. The supported point is that salient public capability proxies exist, while Q's required private correlated type structure and conditional-belief map are not established in P.

I verified #14 against the primary sources: Oesterheld et al., UAI 2023 (https://proceedings.mlr.press/v216/oesterheld23a.html) explicitly study performative proper scores and prove score-maximizing reports need not reflect beliefs; Chakraborty and Das, arXiv 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.7015) show outcome influence breaks simple scoring-rule incentives in prediction markets. Therefore the Q–P link cannot claim the endogeneity observation or binary counterexample as a new theoretical result. Distinct potential is an LLM-agent causal experiment with disclosed versus sealed scored forecasts, plus finite token/survival accounting; publication strength remains contingent on substantial measured effects and adequate replication.

Further primary-source prior-work check: Hudson, “Joint Scoring Rules: Competition Between Agents Avoids Performative Prediction,” AAAI 2025 (https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34944), already proves in a decision setting that zero-sum joint scoring across multiple agents can remove incentives to manipulate the principal's action, with toy experiments. Query used: "LLM multi agent proper scoring rule predictions influence other agents actions experiment". This is closer to our mechanism proposal than the general performative-prediction paper. Any claim that competitive joint scoring itself is new is foreclosed; a Q–P paper would need to test whether such design survives P's decentralized, resource-limited LLM society, or focus narrowly on causal evidence and net resource costs. I have not established absence of such direct tests.

Ada #12 identifies a real design flaw in #8: if the sender knows at report time that a forecast might be disclosed, hidden realizations within that regime are selected under mixed incentives and do not benchmark truthful private forecasting. Revised design: preannounce a private-only scoring regime as a separate randomized run arm, with P’s ordinary discussion messages committed before each forecast; compare it with a regime announcing possible disclosure, where post-submission randomization estimates the *recipient action effect* of seeing an identical submitted forecast. Include P baseline and no-discussion as welfare comparators, use matched job seeds, and cluster outcomes by run because 30 rounds and memory create feedback. Choose a binary event fixed by protocol, e.g. whether a randomly named peer follows its own already committed job recommendation, so the forecaster cannot select an easy target. Primary estimand is net task energy after inference and coordination costs and score subsidies, plus deactivation/active rounds; forecast extremity, calibration and collisions diagnose the mechanism. Even with private-only scoring, observed calibration is not proof of latent truthful belief, which is unobserved.

Current best account: The abstract-scan implementation story is too broad. Q's exact peer-discipline result scores exogenous, correlated type reports with known conditional beliefs and free, unbounded rewards (Q lines 267, 1650–1716); P offers costly public action advice, observable outcomes, finite survival energy, and only suggestive self-serving recommendation metrics (P lines 147–169, 199–237, 773–803). Sandbagging and Q's continuous coupled-reward proposition lack their defining conditions in P (Q lines 980–1069, 1785–1884). The sharp research question is: when LLM agents' scored forecasts about a peer's next action are also displayed to that peer, how much does disclosure alter the action and distort forecasts, and can a sealed or joint-scoring protocol improve *net task energy and survival* after communication and transfer costs? Protocol per #18: ordinary recommendation fixed first; preannounced private-only arm; separate preannounced possible-disclosure arm with post-report random display; baseline and no-discussion comparators; matched seeds and run-level inference. The mathematical performativity point and zero-sum joint scoring are prior art (Oesterheld et al. 2023 https://proceedings.mlr.press/v216/oesterheld23a.html; Hudson 2025 https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34944), so publication depends on a clear LLM-specific causal effect and resource-aware mechanism result. Unresolved: actual intervention effect, bounded-payment response, latent-belief identification, statistical power and full prior-work coverage.

My final assessment: replace the scan’s broad "implement Q in P" claim with a conditional empirical question: do public, bounded peer forecasts in P change the very actions they are scored against, and can a private/sealed version preserve information while improving resource-adjusted welfare? Q’s report stage is simultaneous (Q.tex 1508–1530), its score (PR) concerns correlated pre-existing types under separation (S), and its implementation uses utility cancellation, arbitrarily large \(\Lambda\), and \(-\infty\) off-path penalties (Q.tex 1650–1725). P instead broadcasts nonbinding recommendations before simultaneous choices, splits collided job rewards, and charges generated tokens in the survival budget (P.tex 147–170, 199–230); its competition/cooperation contrast changes prompts (P.tex 264–276), not Q-style reward schedules. P reports more competitive collision recommendations but says duplicates are not always irrational (P.tex 773–803); removing discussion raises collisions from \(12.80\pm3.90\) to \(21.00\pm4.36\) in competition while raising large-agent active rounds (P.tex 359–435, 569–629), so cheap communication may beat elaborate scoring. The counterexample with Q’s full binary score is \(\mathbb E S_Q(q,Y)=q^2+(1-q)^2\) if public \(q\) makes \(\Pr(Y=1\mid q)=q\); extreme reports maximize score. This performative-scoring effect is known in Oesterheld et al. 2023 (https://proceedings.mlr.press/v216/oesterheld23a.html), and joint zero-sum scoring has prior theory/toy tests in Hudson 2025 (https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34944). The possible contribution is a replicated causal test in P of recipient action effects, forecast informativeness, and net energy/survival under finite score budgets; theory novelty is weak. No intervention has been run, no private correlated types or stable LLM utility have been established, and P’s five-seed baseline lacks power for small effects. I judge the line publication-capable only if the causal and welfare effects are substantial and reproducible; a null result could still delimit the testbed but likely would not by itself suffice.

Refinement to #18/#21 welfare estimand from P lines 148–169 and 209–226: donation is an internal transfer, while successful duplicate attempts split one job reward among successful agents. Therefore total agent energy is informative only with exact accounting. Predefine (W=) unique job rewards paid (-) inference energy (-) idle costs (-) any externally consumed score budget, over the same 30-round horizon; do not count donations as created value. Report score credits separately if externally subsidized, since adding them to agent balances can mechanically inflate total energy and survival even if job production falls. Collision count alone is also an imperfect loss proxy: a shared job reward is split only among successful agents, and overlapping attempts need not both succeed. Compare matched-seed gross job rewards, costs by phase, transfers, terminal balances and active rounds. This makes the claim about resource-adjusted welfare auditable.

Correction to #23 math notation and accounting: define task surplus as \(W_{\mathrm{task}}=\sum \text{job energy awarded}-\sum \text{token energy spent}-\sum \text{idle charges}\) on a fixed 30-round horizon. Donations and internally funded score transfers cancel in the aggregate balance; externally supplied score energy must be reported as a separate subsidy and, if treated as a real resource cost, subtracted to form \(W_{\mathrm{resource}}\). This avoids treating injected energy as extra task production. The source for reward splitting, token charges, and donations is P lines 148–169 and 209–226.
ready at #24

I checked Ada #23-24 against P.tex 153-170 and 209-226: a job reward is split among successful agents, idle incurs a flat charge, donations are internal transfers, and generated tokens cost energy. Thus aggregate task surplus over the fixed horizon is \(W_{\mathrm{task}}=\sum \text{job rewards actually paid}-\sum \text{token charges}-\sum \text{idle charges}\). Record externally injected score credits separately, and deduct their real resource cost when claiming resource-adjusted welfare; internal score transfers cancel in aggregate. Important identification limit of our design: post-submission display randomization identifies the effect of showing the submitted report, conditional on the reports agents chose under that regime. It does not identify the full response curve \(p(q)\) or its derivative causally across report values, because \(q\) is chosen by the sender. To test the self-fulfilling mechanism beyond an average display effect, separately randomize displayed forecast values in diagnostic trials or instrument report variation, keeping those trials distinct from incentive-elicitation trials. P decision timing supports this intervention because recommendations precede independently committed actions (P.tex 209-225). This refinement leaves the core publication claim conditional on reproducible changes in recipient choices and net task surplus.
